title: Cloud reliability, defined properly
oneliner: A reliable workload stays available through failures, recovers automatically, scales horizontally, and never runs on guessed capacity.
says: He defines reliability as consistent availability for the customer: failures must trigger automatic recovery, you must know the recovery procedures, the workload must scale horizontally to protect availability, capacity must be measured with monitoring rather than guessed, and the workload must survive platform and infrastructure failures.
explained: Notice what this definition is not: it is not 'the system does not break.' Everything breaks. Reliability is about what happens next - whether the failure is even visible to the customer. That is why he pairs every failure with a recovery behavior: automatic recovery, rehearsed procedures, horizontal scaling so one node dying is a non-event.

The most underrated line here is 'you must not guess the capacity.' Capacity planning is a measurement discipline, not intuition. Monitoring tells you the real headroom; provisioning follows the data. Teams that guess either waste money on idle capacity or discover their real limits during a traffic spike - which is to say, in front of customers.
takeaway: Reliability = automatic recovery + rehearsed procedures + horizontal scale + measured capacity. If any one is missing, you are relying on luck.
